verses.text: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom one hundred twenty satraps, who should be throughout the whole kingdom;
and over them three presidents, of whom Daniel was one; that these satraps might give account to them, and that the king should have no damage.
Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the satraps, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

Then the presidents and the satraps sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion nor fault, because he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.
Then these men said, We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God.
Then these presidents and satraps assembled together to the king, and said thus to him, King Darius, live forever.

All the presidents of the kingdom, the deputies and the satraps, the counselors and the governors, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a strong decree, that whoever shall ask a petition of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it not be changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which doesn’t alter.
Therefore king Darius signed the writing and the decree.

When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
Then these men assembled together, and found Daniel making petition and supplication before his God.

Then they came near, and spoke before the king concerning the king’s decree: Haven’t you signed a decree that every man who makes a petition to any god or man within thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions? The king answered, The thing is true, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which doesn’t alter.

Then answered they and said before the king, That Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah, doesn’t respect you, O king, nor the decree that you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day.
Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored until the going down of the sun to rescue him.
Then these men assembled together to the king, and said to the king, Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians, that no decree nor statute which the king establishes may be changed.
Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. The king spoke and said to Daniel, Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you.
A stone was brought, and laid on the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting; neither were instruments of music brought before him: and his sleep fled from him.
Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste to the den of lions.

When he came near to the den to Daniel, he cried with a lamentable voice; the king spoke and said to Daniel, Daniel, servant of the living God, is your God, whom you serve continually, able to deliver you from the lions?
Then Daniel said to the king, O king, live forever.
My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, I have done no hurt.

Then was the king exceeding glad, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

The king commanded, and they brought those men who had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions mauled them, and broke all their bones in pieces, before they came to the bottom of the den.
Then king Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you.

I make a decree, that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; for he is the living God, and steadfast forever, His kingdom that which shall not be destroyed; and his dominion shall be even to the end.
He delivers and rescues, and he works signs and wonders in heaven and in earth, who has delivered Daniel from the power of the lions.
So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

footnotes.content: Darius organizes his kingdom carefully: one hundred twenty satraps spread across the realm, answerable to three presidents. It's human prudence at work—order, accountability, no single weak point. Yet here's what strikes me: even the best human arrangement cannot prevent what God allows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel becomes one of three presidents. The king wants no loss, no damage to his treasure—a wish every ruler shares. But Darius doesn't know yet that the man he's trusting will face a test that makes political safety look small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An excellent spirit in him. The text doesn't say excellent education or noble birth, but spirit—the deep kind, rooted in the fear of God. Darius sees it and wants to elevate Daniel further. When God lives in us, others sense it, even when they don't name it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His enemies search for a handle—any failure, any slip. But there's nothing. Faithful, without error or fault. This is the life that makes corrupt men furious: not a life of mere outward obedience, but integrity that holds even when no one is watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They admit it openly: the only way to find a fault is to attack his God. They understand what we often forget—our faith is not separate from our character. Where God is, there is no backdoor for accusation. Their trap must strike at his loyalty to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The conspiracy gathers. 'King Darius, live forever'—they flatter him, wrapping malice in ceremony. The court is so much about appearances: correct words, correct forms, the signs of respect. But God sees the heart beneath the bows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thirty days. No one may petition any god or man but the king. It's a decree designed to flatter Darius into a cage—once he signs, he's trapped by his own law. The conspirators are clever, but they're playing a game God has already won.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The law of the Medes and Persians doesn't alter—what a boast of permanence. Yet permanence made by men always breaks. Only God's Word stands forever, and Daniel's enemies are about to learn that one faithful man's God is mightier than all their laws.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Darius signs. Just three words, but they seal the test. The king doesn't know he's signing Daniel's warrant or his vindication. Neither do we, most days, when we sign our names to the small choices that will reveal what we truly believe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Windows open toward Jerusalem. Daniel kneels three times daily, as he did before—his posture of prayer toward the city of God's house doesn't change because a king commanded it. He chooses obedience to the Lord over safety, his very knees a witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They watch him pray. His faithfulness is no secret—and he knows it won't be. There's a courage in that, a simplicity: he will not hide his God to save himself. Some choices close every door except the one that leads through faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They remind Darius of his own decree, speaking it back to him like a trap closing. The king answers truthfully—yes, it's the law. But truth alone won't save Daniel. Truth paired with a king's weakness can do terrible things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel, of the captive children of Judah. They say it with contempt—a foreigner, a slave's son. Yet they're afraid of him, which is why they speak to the king. Fear often wears the mask of accusation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Darius is displeased—greatly displeased. He wants to save Daniel, laboring until sunset to find a way. A king can move mountains, but not the law he himself has made. Sometimes we learn too late that we've locked ourselves in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They press harder: the law cannot be changed. Darius created an escape route he cannot use. His own words now bind him, and Daniel must pay the price of the king's pride. This is how injustice often works—not through cruelty alone, but through law itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The stone closes the den. But before it does, the king speaks to Daniel: Your God whom you serve continually will deliver you. Even in Darius's doubt, there's a thread of hope. And then the darkness seals the prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king seals the stone with his own signet and his lords'. Everything official, everything locked. They want no doubt that justice—as they call it—has been done. But the God who was with Daniel in captivity isn't locked out by a stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king can't eat, can't sleep. His comfort is stripped away. While Daniel rests in the den, upheld by his God, Darius fasts in his palace, tormented. The guilty man sleeps less soundly than the condemned one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Early morning—the worst hour of anxiety. He rises and goes in haste to the lion's den. His heart already knows what his mind wants to deny: that the sentence he signed was unjust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He cries out—a lamentable voice, the text says. Darius asks if the living God can deliver Daniel from the lions. In the darkness and the dawn, the king's question becomes a prayer. Sometimes we don't find faith until we're desperate enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel's first words: O king, live forever. Even in deliverance, he honors the authority God placed over him. This is the steadiness of his spirit—not arrogance in survival, but faithfulness that remains whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths. Not because Daniel was perfect, but because innocence was found in him—innocence toward the king, faithfulness toward God. The angel worked in silence through the night; faith doesn't always announce itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No harm found on him, because he had trusted in his God. Trust is a word we use lightly until we've lived it in a den. Daniel's flesh is whole because his faith held. And the king at last knows, with certainty, the power of the God of his captive servant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The accusers, their children, their wives—all cast in. The lions don't spare them as they spared Daniel. It's harsh justice, the way of earthly kings. But it shows a truth: those who plot against God's faithful invite the very judgment they meant for others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Darius writes to all peoples, nations, and languages. Peace be multiplied. A pagan king, awed by what he's witnessed, proclaims peace in the name of what his servant's God has done. Sometimes a king learns humility only through seeing the faithfulness he tried to punish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In every dominion, men must tremble before the God of Daniel. The living God, steadfast forever, whose kingdom will not be destroyed. Darius can't make anyone believe this—only witnessing it does that. And he has witnessed it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He delivers and rescues, works signs and wonders. Darius's proclamation becomes a hymn. The king has become a herald of the God he didn't know. One faithful man's trust in the Lord changed a kingdom's eye.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and after, in Cyrus's reign. Readers today hear an echo: faithfulness doesn't end in the lion's den or in vindication. It continues, deepens, flourishes. The one who trusted God in darkness finds his trust honored across the years—in Darius's time and after. So it still is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
